Field studies on the Green bush squirrel (Paraxerus poensis) have provided detailed insights into its life history, particularly regarding reproductive output and developmental milestones. Females typically produce litters containing 1 to 2 pups [N_R_i = 1 to 2 pups], and breeding is thought to occur once or, in favorable years, twice annually, resulting in an average of 1.5 litters per year [F_R_i = 1.5 litters per year]. This modest reproductive rate, measured under the typical thermoneutral conditions of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], aligns with expectations for a small-bodied forest sciurid investing in relatively extended parental care. During the pre-weaning period, the dependent neonates remain entirely within the maternal nest, where they are suckled intensively. The age at weaning, marking the transition to nutritional independence and the cessation of lactation, has been estimated at 50 days after birth [tx = 50 days after birth] when measured at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], a value consistent with that documented in the congeneric Funisciurus congicus.

Reproductive timing in Paraxerus poensis appears tightly coupled to the stable thermal environment of its West African forest habitat. Gestation, encompassing the period from internal fertilisation and subsequent foetal development stage through to parturition, lasts approximately 55 days [tg = approximately 55 days] under an ambient temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This comparatively short gestation period for a rodent of its body size is followed by the birth of highly altricial neonates. At delivery, each newborn weighs approximately 9.91 grams [Wwb = approximately 9.91 grams], a modest mass that underscores the altricial nature of the offspring and the substantial energetic burden subsequently placed upon the lactating female. The newborn pups, entirely dependent on maternal milk and warmth, therefore begin a phase of rapid somatic growth that will continue through the suckling juvenile stage until weaning is achieved.

The pace of post-natal development in the Green bush squirrel is relatively slow, consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic investment before reproductive activation. Puberty, defined as the onset of gametogenesis and the first oestrus, occurs at 128 days after birth [tp = 128 days after birth] when individuals are maintained at a body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This extended interval from birth to sexual maturation, a value again based on patterns observed in Funisciurus congicus, suggests that females defer reproductive activation until a substantial proportion of their asymptotic mass has been achieved. Consequently, the pre-reproductive juvenile and sub-adult period is dominated by foraging and growth, allowing young animals to accumulate the body condition necessary to support the energetic demands of subsequent gravid and lactating periods.

Adult females of Paraxerus poensis attain an ultimate wet weight approximating 134 grams [Wwi = 134 grams], although field surveys collated by the Global Biodiversity Information Facility report a range spanning from 125 to 144.5 grams for fully grown individuals. This ultimate mass, representing the plateau in the growth curve characteristic of reproductively viable adult females, is moderate compared to many other forest-dwelling sciurids. The metabolic cost of maintaining this body size under thermoneutral conditions is reflected in the species' basal oxygen consumption, measured at 127.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 127.5 milliliters per hour] when recorded at the standard body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This resting metabolic rate is consistent with the energetic requirements of a small, arboreal mammal inhabiting the humid lowland forests of West Africa.

Longevity records for the Green bush squirrel indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 7.3 years [am = approximately 7.3 years], a value determined under the stable thermal conditions of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C] and representing the total duration from birth to natural death from senescence. This relatively long lifespan for a sciurid of its body mass is notable, as it permits multiple reproductive seasons over the course of an individual's life. The combination of a moderate litter size, a single annual reproductive frequency in many years, and a prolonged adult lifespan suggests a life-history syndrome characterized by steady, iteroparous reproduction. Each surviving female can thus contribute to population recruitment across several breeding seasons, buffering the species against periods of environmental stochasticity in its forest ecosystem.
